newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Airline officials say Guam airport safe. [CORRECTED 13:24 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Airline officials say Guam airport safe. [CORRECTED 13:24 GMT]

text.p: Representatives of some airlines flying into Guam said on Wednesday the airport was safe.
A Korean Air Lines (KAL) Boeing 747, carrying 254 people, crashed into a hillside near the Pacific island's main airport while landing in heavy rain on Wednesday.
(Corrects to delete reference to two survivors later dying in hospital.)
KAL vice president Lee Tae-won said the failure of a safety device at the airport might have been the cause.
Guam officials have confirmed that the airport's glide slope, a device used for instrument landing during poor visibility, had been out of service for some time.
All Nippon Airways' traffic manager Maruta Harunosuke said he felt the Federal Aviation Authorities (FAA)-regulated Guam airport was safe.
"We've operated here for 10 years and had no accidents and no complaints," Maruta said.
An airline representative at Guam said the pilot of ill-fated Flight 801 should have had ample information to land the aircraft even without the glide slope.
"The glide slope has been out of service for more than four weeks for repair, and KAL has been flying in nightly for four weeks," he said, asking not to be identified.

"The glide slope only enhances an instrument landing system (ILS) and is used towards the latter part of an approach," he said, adding that another part of the ILS, the localiser, which gives information on altitude, was working.
Kim Kun-soo, Guam manager of Asiana Airlines, a South Korean airline, said he was also satisfied with the airport's safety standard.
"Our planes have never had a problem here and I have had no reports from our pilots of any complaints," said Kim.
The chairman of the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board, Jim Hall, said the board had started a probe into the crash.
He told a Seattle news conference that investigators would be looking into airport safety equipment for landing.
The Guam Airport Authority's chief of administrative services, Jackie Marati, said 21 investigators from the NTSB and two from the FAA would arrive by Thursday morning.
